aboutH2: Pacific Trails Sober Living: Men's Second-Stage Recovery Housing in Burnaby, BC
intro: Pacific Trails Sober Living runs two sober living houses for men in Burnaby, Odyssey House and Olympus House. It is second-stage recovery housing, the step after treatment, and not a treatment centre: there is no detox, medical care or clinical program on site. Men live together in a sober, structured home with staff on site 24/7 while they go back to work or school.

The houses are run by Pacific Trails Recovery Society, a registered non-profit society in British Columbia, and were started by Max Niemeyer and Joey McGeough, who are both in recovery. Rent covers food and on-site support. Shared rooms start at $1,500 a month.

pillars.title: Odyssey House and Olympus House in South Burnaby
pillars.body: Odyssey House feels like a big family home. The living room is where people end up in the evening, and there is a home gym, a patio, two balconies and a backyard with a koi pond, fire pit and BBQ. Olympus House is the newer, more upscale one, close to Edmonds Town Centre, with bright lounges, a shuffleboard table, a long dining table, a jetted tub and a back patio. Both have single and double rooms and two kitchens. Buses stop outside each house, SkyTrain is a short walk away and Metrotown is about five minutes by car.

pillars.title: Structure That Leaves Room for Work and School
pillars.body: Pacific Trails is abstinence-based. Residents agree to random drug and alcohol testing, do a daily chore and take part in three recovery activities a week on a path they choose, whether that is mutual support meetings, counselling or something else. Everyone sits down for the weekly family dinner and house meeting. Curfew is midnight Sunday to Thursday and 1 a.m. on weekends, and residents can ask for a weekend pass or one longer pass a month. Outside of that, the week belongs to work, school and rebuilding a life in the Lower Mainland.

pillars.title: Started by Two Men Who Have Lived It
pillars.body: Joey McGeough got sober in 2015 after years of heroin and later fentanyl addiction, and has worked in the recovery field for over 10 years. He is a recovery coach and a certified personal trainer, and spent four years as vice president of the Rec Recovery Soccer Association. Max Niemeyer went through treatment in Colorado, moved to Vancouver and lived in a second-stage house himself, where he saw how many men lacked steady support and real friendship. Senior residents mentor newcomers, and the weekly hikes, ski days and fishing trips are part of the plan.

overview: Second-stage housing gives people a place to practise what they learned in treatment. Pacific Trails explains it this way: going straight from an intensive program back to an old environment can trigger a relapse, so a sober home with accountability and peer support bridges the gap. Most men arrive after completing primary treatment, and the team tries to have a room ready the day they finish.

afterOverview: Residents can add outside help if they want it. Pacific Trails points people to Crossing the Threshold for sober coaching and counselling, Missing Link Recovery Solutions for amino acid therapy and nutrition counselling, West Coast Counseling and Neurofeedback Clinic, and The Healing Key Way. These are separate organizations that charge their own fees. The Lower Mainland also has plenty of outpatient programs, recovery sports leagues and daily mutual support meetings within reach of both houses.

location.heading: Pacific Trails Sober Living in Burnaby, British Columbia
location.intro: Pacific Trails has two houses in South Burnaby in Metro Vancouver, each with buses at the door and SkyTrain a short walk away, and Olympus House is steps from Edmonds Town Centre. Downtown Vancouver is about 25 to 30 minutes by car or Expo Line, Surrey and Coquitlam are about 20 to 25 minutes, Abbotsford in the Fraser Valley is about 50 minutes, and Victoria is about 3.5 hours including the Swartz Bay to Tsawwassen ferry.

faqIntro: Answers come from the Pacific Trails website and its public listings. Still unsure? Call, it's free and confidential.

faqs.q: Is Pacific Trails Sober Living a treatment centre?
faqs.a: No. Pacific Trails is men's sober living, which it also calls second-stage recovery housing, in Burnaby, BC. It offers a sober, structured home with 24/7 on-site support and peer support, but no detox, medical care or clinical treatment program. Most residents arrive after finishing primary treatment elsewhere.

faqs.q: How much does Pacific Trails Sober Living cost?
faqs.a: Shared rooms start at $1,500 a month, according to the Pacific Trails website, and single rooms are available at a higher rate. Rent includes food, 24/7 on-site support, the weekly family dinner and house meeting, and use of the shared spaces. Call (604) 992-8174 for current availability and exact pricing.

faqs.q: Who can live at Pacific Trails?
faqs.a: The houses are for men in early recovery who are committed to sobriety. Most come straight from a primary treatment program, but the team says every situation is different and asks people to get in touch. Living there is voluntary, so the applicant has to sign the application even when a counsellor or treatment centre sends it.

faqs.q: What are the two houses like?
faqs.a: Odyssey House in South Burnaby has a large living room, a home gym, a patio, two balconies and a backyard with a koi pond and fire pit. Olympus House is the upscale option near Edmonds Town Centre, with bright lounges, shuffleboard and games, a long dining table, a jetted tub and patios. Both have single and double rooms and two kitchens.

Residents stay fully abstinent from alcohol and drugs and agree to random drug and alcohol testing. Each person does a daily chore, takes part in three approved recovery activities a week and attends the weekly family dinner and house meeting. Curfew is midnight Sunday to Thursday and 1 a.m. on Friday and Saturday.

faqs.q: Do I have to follow a 12-step program?
faqs.a: No. Residents pick their own path and complete three approved recovery activities a week. Pacific Trails says each person can define spirituality in their own way, and it respects any sincere path that supports recovery. The house is abstinence-based.

faqs.q: How long do residents usually stay?
faqs.a: Pacific Trails' recovery.com profile gives a typical stay of 6 to 12 months. Residents quoted on the centre's own website stayed anywhere from about three months to six months before moving into their own place, so length depends on the person.

faqs.q: Where is Pacific Trails and how do I get there?
faqs.a: Both houses are in South Burnaby in Metro Vancouver. Buses stop outside each house, SkyTrain is a short walk away and Metrotown is about five minutes by car. Downtown Vancouver is roughly 25 to 30 minutes by car or Expo Line, and Surrey is about 25 minutes.

faqs.q: Can I spend time away from the house?
faqs.a: Yes. Residents can ask the house manager for a weekend pass covering Friday and Saturday night, plus one extended pass of about a week each month. Passes are usually granted as long as the plan does not put the person's recovery at risk.

Pacific Trails is operated by Pacific Trails Recovery Society, a registered non-profit society in British Columbia, and residents pay monthly rent. Its recovery.com profile says it accepts self-pay as well as band or agency funding. Ask the team directly about funding from a health authority, First Nation or other agency.

Start with a call, text or email to (604) 992-8174 or info@pacifictrailsrecovery.ca. Then download the application form from the website, fill it in and email it back. The team replies within 48 hours and books a screening interview, and men still in treatment are encouraged to apply as early as possible.
